meta.title: The potential adverse effects of hypodermic glucagon-like peptide -1 receptor agonist on patients with type 2 diabetes: A population-based study.
meta.abstract:
Background

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), a class of injectable antidiabetic drugs, have shown significant efficacies in improving glycemic and weight control in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D). However, the long-term safety of GLP-1 RAs remains insufficiently studied. This study aimed to provide real-world evidence on potential adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use in T2D patients without major chronic diseases including impaired cardiac or renal function.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective cohort study involving 7746 T2D patients on GLP-1 RAs in Shenzhen, China. They were compared with 124 371 metformin-only users and 36 146 insulin-only users, forming two therapy control groups. GLP-1 RAs users were also further 1:2 paired with the control groups. Competing risk survival analyses were conducted to assess the incidence risks, presenting subdistributional hazard ratios (sHRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for various adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use.

Results

Compared with metformin-only users, GLP-1 RAs use was associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes (sHRs with 95% CIs), including pancreatitis (2.01, 1.24-3.24), acute nephritis (3.20, 2.17-4.70), kidney failure (3.73, 2.74-5.08), thyroid cancer (2.25, 1.23-4.10), and thyroid dysfunction (1.27, 1.00-1.63), respectively; Similar results were also found when compared with insulin-only users. Importantly, long-term (≥12 months) GLP-1 RAs use may further elevate the incidence risks of pancreatitis, acute nephritis, thyroid cancer, and thyroid dysfunction.

Conclusion

Compared with traditional T2D treatments, GLP-1 RAs use may be associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes in a Chinese population. Cautions were strongly warranted in the use of GLP-1 RAs. Further validation is crucial across diverse populations.

domains.name: Confounding
domains.direction_justification: GLP-1 RA users had higher baseline BMI (13.21% with BMI 30-39.9 vs 4.87% in metformin and 3.04% in insulin) and different socioeconomic/insurance profiles (75.60% citizen health insurance vs 54.96% in metformin). Key prognostic markers such as baseline HbA1c had >90% missingness (90.52% in GLP-1, 91.79% in insulin, 90.45% in metformin) and diabetes duration was not adjusted, leading to unmeasured confounding by diabetes severity and indication pushing risk estimates away from the null.

domains.direction_justification: Exclusion of patients with cumulative co-prescriptions >=6 months across follow-up conditions the cohort definition on post-baseline medication continuation and survival free of early treatment switches, introducing conditioning-on-post-baseline-status bias.

domains.name: Post-exposure interventions
domains.direction_justification: Treating transient acute side effects (such as diarrhea, emesis, acne, dizziness) as competing risk censoring events alters follow-up dynamically based on post-exposure symptom development, with unpredictable direction on hazard ratio estimation.

findings.title: Inappropriate modeling of side effects as competing risks
findings.mechanism: Discontinuation due to acute side effects (e.g., GI distress, emesis) was defined as a competing risk rather than handled via causal mediation or intention-to-treat frameworks.
evidence: Methods state: 'potential competing events were systematically defined as a binomial variable, activated by any incidence of specific acute symptoms, including diarrhea/emesis, dermatitis tetter, acne, dizziness, arrhythmia, etc.'

domains.name: Missing data
domains.direction_justification: HbA1c was missing in over 90% of the analytic cohort (90.52% to 91.79%), fasting glucose was missing in 24.13% to 32.95%, and demographic variables had missingness up to 36%. These were categorized as 'unspecified' rather than imputed or restricted to complete cases, leaving substantial unaddressed missing data bias.

findings.title: Extensive missingness in primary clinical and laboratory variables
findings.mechanism: Unmeasured glycemic control and metabolic severity due to 90%+ missing laboratory values prevents valid adjustment for baseline risk across comparison groups.
evidence: Table 3S note: 'The missing rates of the HbA1c were 90.52%, 91.79%, and 90.45% among GLP-1 RAs, insulin only, and metformin only groups, respectively'
Table 3S note: 'The missing rates of the FPG were 32.95%, 32.66%, and 24.13% among GLP-1 RAs, insulin only, and metformin groups, respectively'

domains.name: Measurement of the outcome
domains.direction_justification: Surveillance and diagnostic workup bias: patients initiated on novel, expensive injectable GLP-1 RAs undergo more frequent clinical monitoring, laboratory workups, and imaging than patients maintained on standard oral metformin, inflating detection of subclinical thyroid nodules/cancer, renal changes, and cysts away from the null.

findings.title: Surveillance and detection bias in electronic health records
findings.mechanism: Outcomes were identified via ICD-10 codes and free-text regex matching in outpatient and inpatient records. Closer clinical surveillance of patients on newly prescribed injectable GLP-1 RAs inflates recorded diagnosis rates compared to stable metformin users.
evidence: Outcomes identified by ICD-10 and regular expression match in outpatient/hospitalization records (Table 2S)
Reported sHRs for surveillance-sensitive outcomes: thyroid cancer sHR 2.25 (95% CI: 1.23-4.10) and thyroid dysfunction sHR 1.27 (95% CI: 1.00-1.63) vs metformin

domains.name: Selection of the reported result
domains.direction_justification: Testing over 20 diverse adverse health outcomes across multiple subgroups (duration <12 vs >=12 months, individual drug agents) without pre-registration or multiple testing correction inflated false-positive significant findings away from the null (e.g., leukemia sHR 15.09 [95% CI: 4.65-48.98]).

findings.title: Multiple testing and outcome dredging without multiplicity adjustment
findings.mechanism: Evaluating multiple organ systems and dozens of ICD-10 diagnostic categories across exposure duration thresholds (<12 vs >=12 months) creates high risk of reporting selective significant extremes driven by small event numbers.
evidence: Observation of an extreme risk for leukemia (sHR 15.09, 95% CI: 4.65-48.98 for >=12 months vs metformin; sHR 6.88, 95% CI: 2.06-22.94 vs insulin), which authors note is 'interpreted cautiously due to the random bias caused by a relatively low incidence rate and cases'

overall.summary: The study exhibits a very high overall risk of bias under ROBINS-E. Major methodological flaws include severe confounding by indication and diabetes severity, exclusion of over 90% of laboratory data (HbA1c missing >90% and handled as missing categories in matching), conditioning cohort selection on post-baseline medication adherence across the entire follow-up period, surveillance bias in electronic record outcome ascertainment, and multiple testing across dozens of outcomes producing implausible estimates (e.g., leukemia sHR 15.09). These biases collectively threaten any causal conclusions regarding the adverse effects of GLP-1 RAs.

unresolvable_without_more_data: Absolute event counts and incidence rates per 1,000 person-years for each specific adverse outcome in GLP-1 RA, insulin, and metformin cohorts (only subdistribution hazard ratios and 95% CIs were provided in the text and tables).

Complete baseline laboratory data (HbA1c, baseline eGFR/serum creatinine, and lipid profile) to evaluate baseline renal status and disease severity without relying on missingness indicator categories.
Data on clinical visit frequency and diagnostic testing frequency (e.g., thyroid ultrasound, renal panels) during follow-up to quantify and adjust for surveillance bias.
